html:
The Thirty Tyrants were a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens for about eight months in 404 and 403 BCE, after Athens lost the Peloponnesian War.

Lysander of Sparta installed them, with a Spartan garrison on the Acropolis. Their leading figure was Critias, a relative of Plato. They limited citizen rights to three thousand favoured men, disarmed the rest and killed about 1,500 people, many of them rich resident foreigners whose property they seized. When the moderate Theramenes objected, Critias had him executed. Socrates stayed in the city, but refused their order to help arrest an innocent man.

Exiled democrats led by Thrasybulus seized a fort at Phyle, then marched on Piraeus and beat the Thirty's forces there; Critias was killed. The Spartan king Pausanias brokered a settlement, and democracy was restored in 403 BCE. Athens passed a general amnesty forbidding prosecutions for what had happened, one of the first known in history. Four years later, the memory of Critias, once Socrates' pupil, hung over the trial of Socrates.
sum: The Thirty Tyrants were a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens for about eight months in 404 and 403 BCE, after Athens lost the Peloponnesian War.
